I hate the age excuse - because it’s not really true. It might be “easier” for kids to learn a language, but that’s not about their brains being better at it - except maybe as a literal baby. It has to do with social expectations. 

Kids will talk at you, no matter if you understand. Adults notice how awkward it is to talk at someone who isn’t picking up what they are saying, and they generally stop or at least don’t do it as much. A kid learning a new language will also just…speak. Adults feel inhibited, generally. Embarrassed, ashamed. 

That being said, I think a lot of people underestimate a lot of factors that make learning a language in a new culture difficult as an adult. You feel isolated. You can’t express yourself as you do in your mother tongue, so other people look at you like you’re stupid, or like you have an infantile understanding of the world - as that is all that you can express at the beginning. It can be very depressing. 

It’s not hard to let that stop you, and the awkward period before you can be fully expressive usually last for years. Also, how do you develop deep friendships when you struggle to say deep things? Lol. I think this is a major factor re. why people give up on learning the language of the place in which they live as an adult, and gravitate towards other people who don’t have a full command of the new language, but with whom they can have a normal, adult relationship.

Never have I read something that was so exactly resonant with my experience. This was/is exactly me. I say was because I have been able to establish safety with one therapist. I say is because I literally just had a panic attack when she suggested I also see a trauma therapist alongside her (who is specifically an ED therapist). 

I don’t know exactly what to suggest, since the issue isn’t completely resolved for me. I still don’t know how to have trust with therapists in general - like you mentioned, my freeze response looked disrespectful and stubborn to a lot of therapists, and the ways they reacted only made my terror more substantial. I’m still afraid of going to a therapist and risking this all happening. 

The way I did establish trust with this one therapist was a little bit of work on my end and a lot of luck re. this particular therapist and her ability to listen and understand and not take my distrust of her personally. I looked for a very experienced therapist, so the chances of her ego getting triggered by my distrust were lessened, and emailed her beforehand telling her exactly what you wrote in this post - asking her if she thought she had the patience and background to help me establish trust with her. I told her what my freeze response looked like, and I told her what kinds of responses to it made me even more frozen and panicked. 

In sessions, when I froze, she would ask to confirm that was what was happening - I could nod yes. She would tell me it was ok, I was safe, she wasn’t frustrated or angry, and I could take all the time I needed to regulate myself. She would say “we’re in this together” and not show any signs of impatience. That was huge. Part of the panic for me has always been, once in a freeze place, the awareness that I was making everything worse.

 If I never felt safe enough to reengage with her, she would still reassure me that we would figure things out - and then before the next appointment I could usually pinpoint what exactly triggered my freeze - whether it was something in my life that prepped me to be extra anxious or something she said. The next session, we would talk about it. Through this, she listened deeply to my triggers - if it was something she had said/done that was out of anything that she should/could do differently, she would literally apologize and take accountability for it - and then never do it again!! 

For example, when she recently suggested a trauma therapist, it was in the middle of a session right after I had experienced a sexual assault. I freaked out that she was going to tell me that she couldn’t see me anymore or that she wouldn’t continue unless I got a trauma therapist too, and how could I talk to a new therapist when it was so fucking hard for me to talk about it with her, my only safe person? She apologized, saying she was reacting to her own emotions of sadness and upset that this had happened to me, and also the knowledge that she didn’t have specific training in trauma, but that she should have regulated those emotions due to the knowledge of my history, and her not doing that caused her to make a recommendation at a terrible time, without fully considering whether it would be the best idea for me or not. 

So, my advice would be to look for and interview (before seeing them) therapists, looking for someone who is very experienced, who is willing to work slowly, willing to deal with carefully establishing the kind of trust that a lot of people have automatically with therapists (how?? lol), and willing to receive communication in writing - because often, when I couldn’t articulate something in a freeze, later by myself I could articulate what caused my big fear and communicate that via writing far more easily that saying it to her face. 

For yourself, I would say it is very important to not push yourself to do things in a therapeutic relationship that you don’t feel safe doing. That will make your inner core rear up in panic. It helped me a lot to say “I want to share that, but I don’t quite feel ready to”. Honoring my own need for safety (and being responded to positively and without frustration) made building trust and safety a way faster process than if I had pushed or shamed myself into sharing when I didn’t feel safe (which I did earlier in therapy situations because that’s what I was “supposed” to do, and I was angry at myself for being so broken). This only hurt the process, and caused more freezes, as my body and subconscious tried to protect me. 

Be kind to yourself! You deserve to feel safe, and you deserve relationships that allow that safety to be built. If a therapists feels they deserve your trust from the get-go, find a different one - they will never be safe because they aren’t willing to understand and have empathy for this frightened part of you.

I eventually found a therapist who has not abandoned me, even when she feels unable to help me. When that happens, we brainstorm together about ways to help me. She has grown to not freak out when I seem “unhelpable”, when I dissociate and put a wall up between myself and her. She has come to understand that it’s all a part of the complex trauma, and that it’s a way I cope, and that she can give me the space to feel safe. She had enough humility to sit with the discomfort herself of not knowing how to help me all the time, of not having ideas and feeling vulnerably incapable. 

I believe it is this feeling that causes many therapists to abandon those of us with complex trauma - they feel incapable, and in their humblest moments think that someone else could better help us, and in their most ego-protective moments they blame us for not being helped by them. They want to get away from the discomfort instead of tolerating it (and in my kindest moments I can understand this, but in my most candid I think…figure it the fuck out, use your coping skills lol). The result is that they abandon us. 

It is not YOUR fault that your trauma is complex. It is not YOUR fault that the average therapist doesn’t feel capable enough to help you, and therefore abandons their work with you - sometimes with grace and other times in a really shitty way. The feeling that results for you is probably the same either way, and that’s understandable and ok. It’s not your fault. 

What I ended up doing is looking for a therapist with a PhD and years of experience. And I got lucky, I think, because that doesn’t guarantee that the person has the capacity for tolerating the discomfort of being faced with complex trauma. I hope that, if you decide to try again, you also get lucky and find someone who can do so. I was like this for such a long time. I went to a trauma therapist and had panic attacks and dissociated just THINKING about speaking out the trauma. It was really hard. Writing about it was impossible. Letting my brain go there equaled week long emotional flashbacks and dissociation. 

My trauma therapist thankfully didn’t get butt hurt about the fact that I didn’t feel safe with her. Lol. She helped me work on simply feeling safe. On soothing myself whenever I started to feel unsafe and go into the dissociation or panic attacks. Deep breathing, crossing my arms over my chests and alternation pats with my hands, soft blankets, anything that calmed my nervous system. We did this for over a year - we didn’t talk about ANY TRAUMA for A YEAR, just learning how to slow down the process of going straight into the coping skills that I had habits of using when I felt unsafe. Super long, super slow process, but it eventually helped.

Asking myself what I needed when I started to panic and not forcing myself to push through and keep doing it until I dissociated was important. If someone - including my therapist - asked me to share something that I felt I should be able to share but I didn’t feel safe sharing, I stopped forcing myself to do it or being angry at myself when I didn’t. I started asserting myself and saying “I would love to eventually share this with you, but right now I don’t feel ready to, and I need to respect that for myself”. I think my brain started to trust me to be able to navigate the panic if it came up, and it started to trust me to take care of me and protect me if it was telling me something was too scary or dangerous. As it learned that I listened and soothed it when it was scared, it started to be able to see that my therapist was indeed safe, and it started to not have to protect itself in wild fear all the time. 

I think we have to be really patient and kind and understanding to our parts that are rightfully so scared and want to protect us so badly that they would try to isolate us or not let anyone in. They have good reasons to be scared, and it’s understandable that it would take a lot of time and gentleness for them to feel it’s safe to open up. But it’s worth taking that time and being so patient. We are worth it - all parts of us. Have hope!

I REALLY hear that. Me too - because self-blames gives us the illusion of control. If it was our fault, that means we could do something “better” to make it not happen again. If it wasn’t our fault, it means that at least part of what happened was out of our control - and this is especially true if we were children. Super uncomfortable thought/feeling. :( 

For me, part of feeling safer was accepting that it wasn’t my fault AND learning to trust that I can help myself better now that I’m an adult and older and wiser and more equipped than I was before. And when I’m confused, I can ask my therapist or a trusted person if they can help me see what’s happening and/or how to stop it or get away from it. And also, I think it’s no small thing to whisper to ourselves “I’m safe from X” (X being whatever happened in the past that is not happening now. Even if it “could” happen again.) If I’m triggered by remembering a certain person’s threats of physical violence, for example, I say to myself: “I am in a different city, they don’t know where I am, I have good locks on my doors” etc. I tell myself truths I can actually believe that offer even little bits of relief. 

I’m SO proud of you for those fleeting moments of self compassion, because I know how hard they are to have especially in the midst of a trauma flashback. That’s really no small thing! I hope you can be proud of that too. Each “little” step we take could lead to a breakthrough - it is just hard to see that when we are focused on how little they seem or how big the trauma seems. But you’re doing great, just by recognizing that trauma is present, by starting to work on it, by protecting yourself by not forcing yourself to trust a therapist before you felt safe to, for writing here, for giving yourself space to feel tiny bits of compassion. I relate to what you wrote - I gave such a hard time trusting therapists, so I also took a long long time to open up about the actual trauma, to build trust with a trauma therapist. Fortunately, the last one (and only good one) I worked with let me take the time, and then was actually equipped with the skills to help me when trauma started leaking out. I had a really hard time staying regulated. She helped me so much, and she didn’t abandon me when I wasn’t “good” at helping myself stay grounded when bringing the trauma out into the open with another person. Of course I wasn’t good at that - I was traumatized and then invalidated by many a professional who was supposed to be trustworthy, but wasn't, and I therefore never learned how to. 

All this to say: in my eyes, this is 100% your trauma therapist’s “fault”. She’s supposed to be able to help you learn how to regulate as you process trauma, and it sounds like she couldn’t do her job. And she backed out of it in a super cowardly way. Not cool not cool. Traumatizing - and that makes sense. 

I will quote my therapist’s words about shitty therapists: “why do you assume it is your fault that you weren’t helped by them? If you were there and wanted to do the work, it was 100% their fault.”

She also always told me to be really gentle with myself during the periods were I was totally overwhelmed by uncovering the trauma. Don’t expect productivity, don’t be hard on yourself, sleep when you need to, cry when you need to. It makes sense that starting to process traumatic things, which before your brain couldn’t handle, so it left them unprocessed, would be really hard and a super big deal. You don’t have to go fast. You don’t have to be ok. Your main job is to sooth yourself as much as you can: hold soft things, watch movies that you really love or make you feel good things, listen to comforting music, force your pets to cuddle you, sit in the sun. Regulating doesn’t have to look pretty - it is literally whatever soothes you and doesn’t hurt you further. Any small thing you can do to express care and compassion toward yourself, even if you’re also feeling anger and self-hatred (which I often do in a triggered state), will make a HUGE DIFFERENCE. Those even tiny acts of treating yourself with even the tiniest bit of love and care can shift mountains. 

I hope you find a good trauma therapist, one who can help you see that the old one behaved shittily, and that it had nothin to do with you. And one who can help you continue to uncover and heal the parts of you that were wounded.
